title: Paid in Advance
subtitle: Port Calloway, Monday Night to Friday, October 1952

listing.title: Paid in Advance 🌧️
listing.blurb: Port Calloway, 1952: rain on the ferries, a freeway tearing through the old waterfront, an election on Tuesday. On Monday night the district attorney puts five hundred dollars on your desk and says someone will kill him on Friday. Find out who before the clock runs out, then decide whether he deserves to be saved, and what to do with the truth. Levels 3–6.

synopsis: Port Calloway is a wet, proud, second-rank Pacific port of four hundred thousand people on the Calloway Sound, a city of ferries, fish, lumber, and men who remember the strikes. In the autumn of 1952 it is tearing itself open. The state is cutting the Shoreline Viaduct, a double-decked freeway on concrete legs, straight through the Tin Mile, the old cannery waterfront, and the money for the land under it is the biggest pile of cash the city has ever seen. On Tuesday 4 November the city votes, for Eisenhower or Stevenson on the radio and, closer to home, for district attorney: the incumbent, Wendell Sloane, tough on the waterfront, endorsed by the Evening Courier and the hilltop money, against Miriam Holloway, a former public defender endorsed by the morning Ledger, which is at war with the Courier over everything. On Monday 27 October, at a quarter to ten at night, Wendell Sloane climbs four flights of stairs to a private detective agency in the Kittredge Building, puts five new hundred-dollar bills on the desk, and says that somebody is going to kill him on Friday and he wants to know who. He is paying in advance. He is lying about almost everything else. Five years ago, as a young assistant DA, Sloane sent a union organizer named Daniel Kessling to the gas chamber for the Halvorsen Cannery fire of 1946, in which eleven people died. Sloane knew Kessling was innocent: he had a signed statement from the cannery's night watchman saying he had been paid to leave his post by the plant manager of Cornelius Vantreight, the man who owned the cannery, the insurance and, ever since, Wendell Sloane. Sloane buried the statement, kept a carbon, and has been bleeding Vantreight with it for five years. Now someone else has a copy. Friday is the fifth anniversary of the execution, the night of Sloane's election-eve rally at the Regent Theatre, and at least four people in Port Calloway have plans for it: Kessling's daughter, who wants the truth said out loud; a waterfront boss whom Sloane's grand jury is about to betray; Vantreight, who has hired a professional and a frame; and Sloane's own wife, who has a train ticket and the original. The detectives have four days, Tuesday to Friday, one scenario each. Everyone has a reason. Nobody is clean. The players decide whether the man who paid them lives, who goes down for it, and whether the truth about the Halvorsen fire ever reaches the front page.
hook: Port Calloway, Monday 27 October 1952, a quarter to ten at night. It has rained since Thursday. The neon of the Rexall sign across Marrow Street is coming through the blinds of the fourth-floor office of Embry Confidential Investigations in the Kittredge Building, and somebody is coming up the stairs because the elevator stops at six. He is tall, grey at the temples, in a good wet overcoat, and every one of you knows his face from the Courier's front page and the posters on every lamppost from the ferry terminal to Larch Hill: SLOANE KEEPS CALLOWAY SAFE. District Attorney Wendell Sloane takes off his hat, shakes the water off it, and lays five new one-hundred-dollar bills on the blotter in a neat fan. He says that somebody is going to kill him on Friday. He says he does not know who. He says he cannot go to the police, because in this city the police are a branch of whoever paid them last. He says he wants a name by Friday, and that the rest of the fee, the same again, is payable on Saturday if he is alive to pay it. Then he says, with a politician's smile that does not reach his eyes, that he is paying in advance because he has always found it concentrates a man's mind. He leaves an envelope with the threat in it. In the street below, a black Hudson with two men in it has been parked with its engine running since he arrived.

setting.name: Port Calloway, Calloway Sound, Monday 27 to Friday 31 October 1952
setting.description: Port Calloway is fictional; the year is real. It sits on a fist of hills above a grey sound on the Pacific Northwest coast, a city built on salmon canning, lumber and shipping, and it still smells of all three when the wind is off the water. The Korean War is in its third year and the shipyards are busy again. Television arrived last year and there are aerials on the roofs of Larch Hill and nowhere else. The city's geography is its class system. Downtown, on the flat between the hills and the harbour, has the Hall of Justice, the County-City Building with the Hall of Records, the Hotel Meridian, the Regent Theatre, and the two newspapers glaring at each other across Commerce Street: the morning Ledger, reforming and broke, and the Evening Courier, owned by Cornelius Vantreight and fat with department-store advertising. West of downtown, along Front Street and Piers 6 to 12, is the Tin Mile: two miles of canneries, net lofts, chandlers, taverns, rooming houses, the hall of Local 9 of the Cannery and Waterfront Workers, and the burned-out Halvorsen Cannery on Pier 9, which nobody has rebuilt in six years. Over the Tin Mile the Shoreline Viaduct is rising on concrete legs, and every week another block is condemned, bought, bulldozed and paid for. South are the Flats, the harbour's working end: boatyards, the Harbor Social Club, a waterfront boss's kingdom. East, up a hill so steep the cable car still runs, is Larch Hill, old money in shingle mansions, the Calloway Club and the Vantreight house, Greyholme, looking down on all of it. Fifty minutes across the sound by steam ferry is Gannet Island, farms, fog and the St. Agnes Sanatorium. The city is mixed and always has been: Scandinavian fishing families, Filipino and Chinese cannery crews who have worked the Tin Mile for three generations, Japanese-American families back from the camps and rebuilding their shops on Jackson Street, Black shipyard workers who came in the war and stayed, Okies, Irish cops, Italian grocers. They are neighbours, union brothers and voters, and they are the people the freeway is being built over.
setting.atmosphere: Rain. Always rain: the fine, endless, sideways Calloway rain that does not fall so much as hang, so that every streetlight has a halo and every collar is wet. Foghorns from the sound at night. The steam ferry's whistle at ten-thirty and two-fifteen. Neon reflected in tramlines. The pile drivers on the viaduct start at seven every morning and the whole Tin Mile shakes. Diners that smell of coffee and fried clams. Payphones that take a nickel. The radio is full of the election, Ike and Adlai, and in every bar someone is arguing about Korea. The tone is hard-boiled paperback, not horror: cigarette smoke, rye, wet wool, a bruise that takes a week to fade, blood on a linoleum floor, a man who tells you the truth because he is too tired to lie. Everyone is compromised and almost no one is a monster. Let the city be a character: the rain should comment on scenes, the viaduct should loom over them, and the newspapers should print what the players did the next morning, wrong.

regions.name: Downtown
regions.description: The flat between the hills and the harbour, and the city's machinery. The Kittredge Building on Marrow Street, eight floors of dentists, bail bondsmen, a dance studio and the agency on the fourth. The Hall of Justice on Commerce Street, with the DA's office on the third floor and police headquarters behind it, and Ambrose Pell's shoeshine stand on its steps. The County-City Building and the Hall of Records in its basement. The Ledger Building, with its newspaper morgue, its switchboard and its presses in the basement, faces the Courier Building across Commerce Street, and the two papers' delivery trucks race each other to every corner at dawn. The Hotel Meridian, twelve floors of faded marble where out-of-town salesmen stay. The Regent Theatre, two thousand seats of gilt and velvet, where Wendell Sloane holds his election-eve rally on Friday night.

regions.name: The Tin Mile
regions.description: Two miles of canneries along Front Street and Piers 6 to 12, and the heart of the city's working past. Fish-scale on the cobbles, net lofts, chandlers, the Seaman's Bethel, tavern after tavern, rooming houses where Nora Kessling grew up. The hall of Local 9, a brick box with a mural of the 1934 strike. The Halvorsen Cannery on Pier 9, a black ruin fenced with wire since the fire of 9 March 1946; eleven people died there. Elmer Dahl's pawnshop on Water Street. Over all of it the Shoreline Viaduct, half built, its concrete legs marching up Front Street, its construction yard full of cranes, rebar and dynamite. Half the Tin Mile has already been condemned. The other half is waiting for the letter.

regions.name: The Flats and the Harbour
regions.description: The south end of the waterfront: boatyards, fuel docks, the ferry terminal at Pier 3, the fish auction at dawn, and the Harbor Social Club, a two-storey clapboard bar and card room on pilings where Gil Maddox runs the shape-up, the numbers and the loading-dock rackets. Maddox's boathouse is a hundred yards along the boardwalk. The Pelican Club, the city's best nightclub, is here too, on a pier of its own, with a band, a singer, a back room and a view of the ferry lights; everyone goes there, which is the point.

regions.name: Larch Hill and Gannet Island
regions.description: Larch Hill is up the cable car from Commerce Street: shingle-and-stone mansions behind laurel hedges, the Calloway Club, Episcopal bells, Packards in the driveways and television aerials on the roofs. Greyholme, the Vantreight house, sits at the top with its back to the sky. People up here say the Tin Mile as if it were a smell. Fifty minutes across the sound by the steam ferry Kittiwake is Gannet Island: fog, dairy farms, a ferry landing with a café, and the St. Agnes Sanatorium, run by nuns, where the night watchman of the Halvorsen Cannery is dying of lung cancer in a room that faces the city he lied to.

campaignRules.name: The Clock
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs on a fixed five-day calendar, Monday night to Friday night, and the opposition acts on it whether or not the players are watching. Each scenario is one day (pa-scenario-001 Tuesday, 002 Wednesday, 003 Thursday, 004 Friday). The unit of time is the scene, about two hours; a day has six to eight scenes from breakfast to the last ferry, and every trip across town, every stakeout and every wait outside an office costs one. Track the time openly. If the players do not interfere, this happens. TUESDAY: Nora Kessling buys a .32 pocket pistol from Elmer Dahl's pawnshop at 11 a.m., and Dahl telephones its serial number to Lt. Ray Dunleavy; Ansel Teague, the professional, checks into the Hotel Meridian as an insurance adjuster; at 2 a.m. Gil Maddox's men steal a case of dynamite from the viaduct construction yard. WEDNESDAY: Nora takes the 10:30 ferry to Gannet Island to get the dying watchman, Oskar Lindqvist, to sign a fresh statement; Frank Lusk's men follow her; at 11 p.m. Dunleavy and Teague meet in the back room of the Pelican Club; at 2 a.m. Teague, sent by Vantreight once Dunleavy hears where Nora went, crosses on a hired launch, and at 3 a.m. he smothers Lindqvist in his bed. THURSDAY: Lindqvist is found dead at 6 a.m.; Constance Sloane withdraws the original Lindqvist statement from her safe-deposit box at 3 p.m. and buys a ticket for Friday's 10:40 train south; Teague rehearses at the Regent in the afternoon; Lusk's men break into Nora's room at 9 p.m. and take her photostat; Maddox's man Vic Dorrance wires the dynamite under the DA's Packard in the county garage at 2 a.m. FRIDAY: at 7 a.m. Dunleavy 'finds' the bomb, as Vantreight wants, and Maddox's arrest is on the Courier's noon edition; the grand jury reports at 10; the viaduct dedication is at noon; Sloane's rally opens at the Regent at 8 p.m. and he speaks at 8:40; Nora stands up in the balcony; Teague fires from the stage-left box; Dunleavy seizes Nora and swaps her .32 for Teague's twin; the Courier's late edition says DA SLAIN, and Constance's train leaves at 10:40. Whatever the players change, the people they have not touched carry on, adapting only to what they could plausibly know.

campaignRules.name: Heat
campaignRules.description: The party has a single Heat score for Port Calloway, 0 to 10, tracked openly by the GM and announced whenever it changes; it starts at 1 because a DA was seen climbing their stairs. It rises by 1 for being seen somewhere you should not be, leaning on the wrong man (a cop, a Larch Hill name, a union officer in his own hall), a fistfight in public or a story with the agency's name in it; by 2 for gunfire, a car chase the police see, or breaking into a building; by 3 for a body. It falls by 1 for each half-day spent quietly, and by 1 when the party does someone powerful a favour. At Heat 3 the cops start asking: Dunleavy's men tail the party and the desk sergeant stops taking bribes. At Heat 6 someone is told to take care of you: Maddox or Vantreight (whichever the party has hurt more) sends men, and the agency's office is searched. At Heat 9 the city is closed to you: the party's licences are pulled, there is a warrant on a pretext, and no doorman, clerk or cabbie will help. Sloane's name does not lower Heat. It raises it, because everyone in the Hall of Justice knows he is in trouble.

campaignRules.name: The Three-Clue Rule
campaignRules.description: Every conclusion the players need to reach has at least three clues pointing to it, in different places, and every scenario names them. Core clues are found automatically by anyone who looks in the right place with the right skill: no roll. Rolls add detail, save time or avoid Heat; a failed roll never dead-ends the case, it costs a scene, a favour or a point of Heat. The campaign's conclusions are lettered A to H in the control file and each scenario lists which clues it holds. If the players are stuck, use the case board: summarize the suspects, what each is known to want, the open questions and the leads not yet followed, out loud, in character if possible (Walt Embry's blackboard, Pip Ashdown's notebook).

campaignRules.name: The Client Lies
campaignRules.description: Wendell Sloane is the client and the victim, and he is not a good man. He lies to the party in the first five minutes and keeps lying: he says he does not know why Friday, he says he has no idea who would want him dead except 'the criminal element', and he says he wants a name to protect himself. What he actually wants is to know who has a copy of the Lindqvist statement, so that he can have it destroyed and that person silenced. Anything the party reports to Sloane, he uses: if they give him Nora Kessling's name, he has Dunleavy pick her up on a pretext the next day; if they mention the sanatorium, Lindqvist is moved or dies sooner; if they tell him about Vantreight, he raises his price. He pays promptly, he is charming, and he is genuinely frightened. The players are never obliged to save him, and never obliged to let him die. That is the campaign's question.

campaignRules.name: Ink and Rain: The Newspaper War
campaignRules.description: The morning Ledger (reform, Miriam Holloway's paper, publisher Hollis Gage) and the Evening Courier (Vantreight's paper, Sloane's paper) print what the party did, the next edition, from their own side. Each scenario ends with two headlines. Whatever the party gives a newspaper is in print within twelve hours and changes the clock: a Ledger story about the Halvorsen fire makes Vantreight move faster and makes Sloane desperate; a Courier story about the agency raises Heat by 1. Getting the truth into print is a legitimate win condition, and the hardest one: the Ledger will not print a dead watchman's word against the city's richest man without the original signed statement or a living witness, and Hollis Gage's lawyer reads every line. Travel: within downtown and the Tin Mile, walking or a cab takes part of a scene; Larch Hill is a cable-car ride or a steep drive; Gannet Island is the Kittiwake ferry from Pier 3 (departs 7:10, 10:30, 2:15 and 5:40; returns 8:40, 12:00, 3:45 and the last boat at 7:10 p.m.) or a hired launch for $20 and a wet hour.

explorationRules: This is a city campaign and the map is a schematic of Port Calloway: downtown on the flat, the Tin Mile and the half-built viaduct to the west, the Flats and the ferry terminal to the south, Larch Hill to the east, Gannet Island across the sound. Within the city the party moves by car (Ruby Tate's Hudson is the party's car if she is played), cab, cable car, streetcar and on foot, and the unit of time is the scene, roughly two hours. The clock (see campaignRules) is the engine: every scene the players spend somewhere is a scene they do not spend somewhere else, and the suspects keep moving. Run each day as a small sandbox of named places, listed in that day's scenario, with each suspect acting on their own schedule and on what they could know. Nobody is omniscient: Vantreight knows what Dunleavy and Sloane tell him, Maddox knows what the waterfront sees, Sloane knows what the party reports. Investigation follows the three-clue rule: core clues are automatic for anyone who looks in the right place with the right skill; rolls only add detail or speed, and failure costs time, Heat or a favour, never the case. Fights are short, ugly and rare; most scenes are conversations in bad light with someone who wants something. Bribes are normal and priced (a doorman $1, a hotel desk clerk $5, a desk sergeant $10, a coroner's report $50); favours are better than cash. Between scenes let the city breathe: the pile drivers at seven, the cannery whistle at noon, the ferry whistle, a radio in a diner arguing about Korea, the smell of the fish auction, a streetcar sparking in the rain. The players should come away knowing what Port Calloway felt like, and feeling a little sorry for it.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. Like a character's hit points, this does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. Port Calloway and every person in it are fictional; the year, the Korean War, the 1952 presidential election, and the general history of West Coast waterfront labour and urban freeway building are real. Eisenhower and Stevenson are on the radio and nowhere else. No real private individual appears. The Halvorsen fire is invented.
controlFile.theTruth: On the night of 9 March 1946, during a cannery strike led by Local 9 organizer Daniel Kessling, the Halvorsen Cannery on Pier 9 burned and eleven people died: nine strike-breakers sleeping in the loft, a foreman and a fourteen-year-old boy who swept the floor. The fire was set for the insurance and to break the strike by Earl Haskin, plant manager for Cornelius Vantreight, who owned Halvorsen Packing through a holding company; Haskin paid the night watchman, Oskar Lindqvist, $200 to be off his post between midnight and two, and paid a torch from out of town whom nobody ever identified. Three days later, frightened and drunk, Lindqvist walked into the DA's office and gave a signed statement to the young assistant DA on duty, Wendell Sloane, typed by Sloane's secretary, Constance Muir. Sloane took it to Vantreight instead of to his boss. Vantreight made Sloane a rich man and, in 1948, district attorney; Sloane charged Kessling, using perjured testimony from Kessling's friend and rival Frank Lusk (who was facing a theft charge Sloane dropped, and who has run Local 9 ever since), and Kessling was executed at the state penitentiary on Friday 31 October 1947, saying he was innocent. Sloane told Vantreight he burned the Lindqvist statement. He kept a carbon in his home safe and has been taking $1,000 a month from Vantreight, through Vantreight's dummy Northgate Land Company, ever since. Constance, who married Sloane in 1948, took the original from his files on the night of the execution and has kept it for five years in a safe-deposit box at Pacific Mercantile Bank, out of guilt and as insurance. This summer, after a bad year in a cold marriage, she mailed a photostat of it anonymously to Kessling's daughter, Nora. Nora found Lindqvist dying at St. Agnes on Gannet Island; he confirmed it to her. On Saturday 25 October Nora mailed Sloane a clipping of the Ledger's story of her father's execution with one word typed under it: FRIDAY. She meant: on Friday, the anniversary, at your rally, I will stand up and say it. Sloane checked his safe, found his carbon, and realised another copy exists. He told Vantreight on Monday afternoon and demanded $50,000 to 'handle it'. Vantreight decided instead that Sloane, who has become greedy, careless and unelectable, is a liability, and that the threat letter is a gift. He brought in a professional, Ansel Teague, and through Lt. Ray Dunleavy (who beat the false confession out of a witness in 1946 and is Vantreight's man in the police) arranged a frame: Dunleavy's informant, the pawnbroker Elmer Dahl, sells Nora a .32 on Tuesday and passes on its serial; Teague carries the identical model. On Friday at 8:40 p.m., when Nora stands up in the Regent balcony, Teague shoots Sloane from the stage-left box, Dunleavy seizes Nora and swaps the guns, and the Courier's late edition, already set in type, says DA SLAIN; RED ORGANIZER'S DAUGHTER HELD. With Sloane dead, the man most able to expose Vantreight is gone, a reform DA is unlikely to reopen a fire whose only witness is dead, and Vantreight's Northgate Land condemnation awards on the viaduct right-of-way, worth $2.3 million and resting on a fraud complaint Sloane's office buried, go through. Meanwhile Gil Maddox, whose arrangement with Sloane is being betrayed by Friday's grand jury report, has his own plan: a bomb under Sloane's Packard. Vantreight knows of it through Dorrance and Dunleavy and wants it found on Friday morning, because a bomb at the viaduct dedication would kill the mayor and the governor's highway commissioner, freeze the federal freeway money and bring the FBI; a bomb found on Friday morning blames the waterfront and leaves the rally to Teague.
suspects: Cornelius Vantreight, 67, Larch Hill: owner of the Courier and Northgate Land, the man who paid for the fire. Motive: Sloane is blackmailing him and is about to cost him $2.3 million and his liberty. Plan: Ansel Teague at the Regent, Friday 8:40, with Dunleavy's frame of Nora. THIS IS THE ATTEMPT THAT SUCCEEDS IF NOBODY INTERFERES.

Nora Kessling, 26, switchboard operator at the Ledger, Daniel Kessling's daughter. Motive: her father. Plan: stand up at the rally with the photostat and say it; give the photostat and Lindqvist's fresh signed statement to Hollis Gage of the Ledger for Saturday's edition. She bought a .32 'for protection' and does not know herself whether she would use it. She sent the letter.

Gil Maddox, 51, waterfront boss, the Harbor Social Club. Motive: for six years he has paid Sloane to leave the shape-up alone, and Friday's grand jury report will indict his two lieutenants so Sloane can look tough before the election. Plan: dynamite under Sloane's Packard, wired Thursday night by Vic Dorrance, to go off when the car starts after the noon viaduct dedication.

Constance Sloane, 44, the DA's wife, formerly his secretary. Motive: a cold, contemptuous marriage, his women, and a $100,000 life-insurance policy in her name; and five years of guilt. Plan: none involving murder. She is leaving on Friday's 10:40 train with the original statement, intending to mail it to Miriam Holloway from the first stop, unless someone gives her a reason to trust them sooner.

Frank Lusk, 49, president of Local 9. Motive: his 1947 perjury; if the truth comes out, he is finished. Plan: not murder. Sloane has quietly ordered him to find who has the paper, and Lusk's men follow Nora to Gannet Island on Wednesday and break into her room on Thursday night to take the photostat. He is the most ashamed man in the city and the likeliest to break.

Lt. Ray Dunleavy, 48, Homicide, assigned to the DA's security for the week. Not a suspect so much as an accomplice: he arranges the gap at the Regent, the gun swap and the arrest, and is the party's main police antagonist. Vantreight has promised him the chief's job.
redHerrings: Constance Sloane's $100,000 insurance policy, her train ticket and her steady hands make her look like a murderess. She is the opposite: the person who started the truth moving. If the party accuses her, she closes up; if they are kind, she is their best witness.

Gil Maddox's bomb is real, and stopping it on Thursday night feels like solving the case. It is designed by the campaign to be a false climax: the party should feel triumphant, and then on Friday morning realise the bomb was supposed to be found.

Frank Lusk's men are following Nora and breaking into her room; they look like killers. They are thugs doing a frightened man's errand, and Lusk himself will, if leaned on with the truth, confess his 1947 perjury.
Ansel Teague is registered as an insurance adjuster and Constance has a large policy; a party may think Teague is investigating her. He has never heard of her policy.
clues: A. THE THREAT IS ABOUT THE 1946 HALVORSEN FIRE AND DANIEL KESSLING'S EXECUTION. A1: the threat is a clipping of the Ledger's 1 November 1947 story of Kessling's execution, with FRIDAY typed under it (pa-scenario-001). A2: the Ledger morgue: Kessling was executed on Friday 31 October 1947, so this Friday is the fifth anniversary (pa-scenario-001). A3: the county archive clerk: Sloane himself signed out the Halvorsen case file on Saturday morning (pa-scenario-001). A4: Miriam Holloway, who defended Kessling, says Sloane 'won a case he should never have been able to win' (pa-scenario-001).

B. SLOANE IS LYING: HE WANTS THE PAPER, NOT THE KILLER, AND HE IS BLACKMAILING VANTREIGHT. B1: the five $100 bills are sequential and still carry a Pacific Mercantile band stamped NORTHGATE LAND CO. (pa-scenario-001). B2: Agnes Ruud, Sloane's secretary: on Monday he told her to list everyone who had asked for the Halvorsen file or for Lindqvist's address since 1946 (pa-scenario-001). B3: Frank Lusk: 'the DA's got me looking for the same thing you are' (pa-scenario-002). B4: Constance: the safe, the carbon, and the monthly envelopes from Larch Hill (pa-scenario-003).

C. NORA KESSLING SENT THE LETTER AND HAS A COPY OF THE LINDQVIST STATEMENT. C1: the FRIDAY was typed on the Ledger switchboard's Underwood, whose capital R prints high (pa-scenario-001). C2: the Ledger morgue's checkout card for the Halvorsen envelope: N. Kessling, five times since July (pa-scenario-001). C3: the St. Agnes visitors' book: N. Kessling, every Sunday since August (pa-scenario-002). C4: Elmer Dahl's pawn ledger: a .32 sold to N. Kessling on Tuesday (pa-scenario-001 or 002).

D. GIL MADDOX PLANS TO BOMB SLOANE'S CAR. D1: a case of dynamite stolen from the viaduct construction yard on Tuesday night; the night watchman saw a Harbor Social Club truck (pa-scenario-001 or 002). D2: Vic Dorrance asked the county garage attendant when the DA's Packard is washed and who has the keys (pa-scenario-003). D3: blasting caps, wire and a dry-cell battery in Maddox's boathouse (pa-scenario-002 or 003). D4: Maddox, drunk, to Rainy Doucette or any singer at the Pelican: 'Wendell's going out with a bang' (pa-scenario-002).

E. VANTREIGHT SET THE FIRE AND SLOANE BURIED IT. E1: the Lindqvist statement itself, photostat (Nora) or original (Constance) (pa-scenario-002 to 004). E2: Lindqvist's own deathbed account, if the party reaches him on Wednesday (pa-scenario-002). E3: Hall of Records: Halvorsen Packing's $310,000 insurance payment and Earl Haskin's $5,000 deposit in April 1946 (pa-scenario-003). E4: Frank Lusk's confession of his 1947 perjury (pa-scenario-002 or 003). E5: Sloane's carbon, in the safe at his house on Alder Terrace (pa-scenario-003).

F. VANTREIGHT HAS HIRED A PROFESSIONAL, AND DUNLEAVY IS IN IT. F1: the Hotel Meridian register: A. Teague, Northwest Casualty Mutual, Portland, room 914, paid by Northgate Land Co. cashier's check (pa-scenario-002 or 003). F2: Dunleavy and Teague in the Pelican Club back room on Wednesday at 11 p.m. (pa-scenario-002). F3: Vantreight's chauffeur, Bertil Moe, drove 'the man from Portland' up to Greyholme on Monday (pa-scenario-003). F4: Lindqvist's murder: petechiae, a pillow, and a launch skipper who took a man in a grey Chesterfield across at 2 a.m. (pa-scenario-003). F5: Dunleavy rewrote the Regent security rota on Thursday to put every honest cop on the front doors (pa-scenario-003 or 004).

G. NORA IS BEING SET UP AS THE PATSY. G1: Dahl's pawn ledger: next to the .32's serial, in pencil, 'phoned Lt. D. 11:20' (pa-scenario-001 or 002). G2: on the street, Dahl is known as Dunleavy's stool pigeon (pa-scenario-002). G3: in Teague's Meridian room, a second Colt .32 pocket pistol of the same model and finish (pa-scenario-003). G4: in the Courier composing room, a Saturday front page already set in type: DA SLAIN; RED ORGANIZER'S DAUGHTER HELD (pa-scenario-003).

H. THE ATTEMPT IS AT THE REGENT AT 8:40 ON FRIDAY, FROM THE STAGE-LEFT BOX. H1: Teague's Regent seating plan, with the stage-left box ringed and 8:40 pencilled on it (pa-scenario-003). H2: the Regent stage-door man was paid $20 by an 'insurance man' to see the fly gallery and the boxes on Thursday (pa-scenario-003 or 004). H3: Dunleavy's security rota leaves the stage-left box and the fly-gallery stair unguarded (pa-scenario-003 or 004). H4: a stakeout of the Regent on Thursday afternoon sees Teague time the walk from the box to the alley door with a stopwatch (pa-scenario-003).
controlFile.theDAsSecretAsKey: The players solve the case when they understand that Friday is about the Halvorsen fire. Once they know that, every motive lines up: Nora wants the truth, Lusk wants it buried, Constance has the original, Vantreight cannot afford it, and Sloane hired them to find it. Point the early clues (A and B) hard. If the party reaches Wednesday without knowing about the fire, have Miriam Holloway, Ambrose Pell or Lindqvist himself put it in front of them.
controlFile.outcomes: There is no single right ending, only consequences. SLOANE: if the party does nothing, he dies at 8:40 on Friday and Nora is charged. If they stop Teague, Sloane lives; whether he wins the election depends on the truth. VANTREIGHT: he is untouchable unless the party has evidence that reaches someone outside his reach: the original statement plus Lusk's confession or Teague alive and talking, given to Miriam Holloway, the Ledger, or the FBI agent on the freeway-fraud detail. Then he is indicted in December, and his Northgate awards are frozen. NORA: cleared if the gun swap is stopped or proved (G clues), otherwise tried, and she becomes the campaign's open wound. THE TRUTH: if the Ledger prints the Lindqvist statement on Saturday 1 November, Sloane loses on Tuesday whatever else happens, the governor posthumously pardons Daniel Kessling in the spring of 1953, and the Tin Mile gets a plaque. If the party sells the paper to Sloane ($5,000) or Vantreight ($10,000), they are rich, Nora is alone, and Heat never quite falls below 3 again. The viaduct gets built either way: it is 1952. The question the campaign asks is not whether the city can be saved, but whether this one thing can be made true in print.
